title: Concurrency vs parallelism — interleaving vs simultaneous, IO-bound vs CPU-bound

s1_definition.profdef: **Concurrency** = multiple tasks make progress by INTERLEAVING their execution. Even on a single CPU core, the OS switches between threads rapidly (time-slicing), giving the ILLUSION of simultaneous execution. Concurrency is about STRUCTURE — dealing with many things at once. **Parallelism** = multiple tasks execute at the EXACT same instant on DIFFERENT CPU cores. Parallelism is about EXECUTION — doing many things at once. Concurrency is possible on 1 core. Parallelism requires multiple cores. **IO-bound tasks** (DB queries, HTTP calls, file reads) benefit from CONCURRENCY — while one thread waits for IO, another uses the CPU. **CPU-bound tasks** (encryption, compression, sorting) benefit from PARALLELISM — multiple cores computing simultaneously. Thread count rule: IO-bound → many threads (cores × 2-10). CPU-bound → cores threads (more threads = context switching waste).
s1_definition.analogy: **Concurrency** = ONE teller juggling 3 customers. Serves customer-A for 1 minute, switches to customer-B while waiting for A's paperwork, switches to C, back to A. All 3 make progress, but only 1 is served at any instant. **Parallelism** = THREE tellers, each serving a different customer AT THE SAME TIME. Truly simultaneous. IO-bound (waiting for vault to open) = concurrency is great (teller does other work while waiting). CPU-bound (counting cash) = parallelism is needed (3 tellers count 3 piles simultaneously).
s1_definition.oneliner: Concurrency = interleaving (structure, 1 core possible). Parallelism = simultaneous (execution, needs multi-core). IO-bound → concurrency (many threads). CPU-bound → parallelism (cores threads).
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** **Concurrency** = multiple tasks make progress by INTERLEAVING their execution. Even on a single CPU core, the OS switches between threads rapidly (time-slicing), giving the ILLUSION of simultaneous execution. Concurrency is about STRUCTURE — dealing with many things at once. **Parallelism** = multiple tasks execute at the EXACT same instant on DIFFERENT CPU cores. Parallelism is about EXECUTION — doing many things at once. Concurrency is possible on 1 core. Parallelism requires multiple cores. **IO-bound tasks** (DB queries, HTTP calls, file reads) benefit from CONCURRENCY — while one thread waits for IO, another uses the CPU. **CPU-bound tasks** (encryption, compression, sorting) benefit from PARALLELISM — multiple cores computing simultaneously. Thread count rule: IO-bound → many threads (cores × 2-10). CPU-bound → cores threads (more threads = context switching waste).

**In simple words (banking analogy):** **Concurrency** = ONE teller juggling 3 customers. Serves customer-A for 1 minute, switches to customer-B while waiting for A's paperwork, switches to C, back to A. All 3 make progress, but only 1 is served at any instant. **Parallelism** = THREE tellers, each serving a different customer AT THE SAME TIME. Truly simultaneous. IO-bound (waiting for vault to open) = concurrency is great (teller does other work while waiting). CPU-bound (counting cash) = parallelism is needed (3 tellers count 3 piles simultaneously).

**One line to remember:** Concurrency = interleaving (structure, 1 core possible). Parallelism = simultaneous (execution, needs multi-core). IO-bound → concurrency (many threads). CPU-bound → parallelism (cores threads).

sections.s3_banking: **Problem — The EOD batch used a single 4-thread pool for BOTH IO-bound (DB queries, API calls) and CPU-bound (encryption, report generation) tasks.** DB queries (200ms wait) occupied all 4 threads → encryption tasks queued for 10 minutes. Fix: TWO pools — `ioPool = newFixedThreadPool(50)` for DB/API calls, `cpuPool = newFixedThreadPool(4)` for encryption. IO tasks use 50 threads (mostly waiting). CPU tasks use 4 threads (fully utilizing 4 cores). Total EOD time: 3 hours → 20 minutes.

sections.s5_journey:
**Step 1 (IO-bound).** 20 tasks each sleep 200ms (simulating DB query). With 20 threads: all 20 start simultaneously → all wait 200ms → all complete at ~200ms total. Sequential: 20 × 200ms = 4000ms.

**Step 2 (CPU-bound).** 100K elements squared. parallelStream splits across 4 cores → each core processes 25K elements → merge. Speedup: ~3-4x on 4 cores.

**Step 3 (Separate pools).** IO pool (20 threads) handles DB queries. CPU pool (4 threads) handles encryption. Neither starves the other. IO tasks don't waste CPU cores. CPU tasks get dedicated cores.
sections.s5b_flow:
```
  ═══ CONCURRENCY vs PARALLELISM ═══

  CONCURRENCY (1 core, interleaving):
  Core: [T1][T2][T1][T3][T2][T1]...
  Tasks interleave on ONE core. Progress by time-slicing.

  PARALLELISM (4 cores, simultaneous):
  Core-1: [T1]────────────
  Core-2: [T2]────────────
  Core-3: [T3]────────────
  Core-4: [T4]────────────
  Tasks truly run at the same instant!

  ═══ THREAD COUNT RULE ═══
  IO-bound (DB, HTTP, file):  threads = cores × (1 + wait/compute) → MANY
  CPU-bound (encrypt, sort):  threads = cores → FEW
  Mixed workload:             SEPARATE POOLS!
```
sections.s5c_hld:
```
  ═══ HLD — Dual Pool Architecture ═══

  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  Banking Service                              │
  │                                                │
  │  IO Pool (50 threads):                        │
  │  ├─ DB queries (200ms wait each)              │
  │  ├─ HTTP calls (payment gateway)              │
  │  └─ File reads (statements)                   │
  │                                                │
  │  CPU Pool (4 threads = cores):                │
  │  ├─ Encryption (AES-256)                      │
  │  ├─ Report generation (PDF)                   │
  │  └─ Hash computation (checksum)               │
  │                                                │
  │  Separate pools → neither starves the other!  │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────┘
```
sections.s5d_lld:
```
  ═══ LLD — Concurrency vs Parallelism ═══

  ┌─ CONCURRENCY (structure) ─────────────────┐
  │  Multiple tasks INTERLEAVE on shared cores │
  │  OS scheduler: time-slicing, context switch│
  │  Benefit: utilize CPU while IO waits       │
  │  Thread count: many (IO wait time >> CPU)  │
  │  Example: 100 DB queries on 4 cores        │
  │  → 100 threads, most WAITING, CPU free     │
  └────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  ┌─ PARALLELISM (execution) ─────────────────┐
  │  Multiple tasks run SIMULTANEOUSLY         │
  │  Requires: multiple CPU cores              │
  │  Benefit: divide work across cores         │
  │  Thread count: = cores (more = waste)      │
  │  Example: encrypt 1M records on 4 cores    │
  │  → 4 threads, each processes 250K          │
  └────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  Thread count formula:
  IO-bound:  N = cores × (1 + W/C)
    W = wait time (200ms), C = compute time (10ms)
    N = 4 × (1 + 200/10) = 4 × 21 = 84 threads
  CPU-bound: N = cores = 4 threads
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
Concurrency is about structure — multiple tasks making progress by interleaving, possible on a single core via time-slicing. Parallelism is about execution — multiple tasks running at the exact same instant on different cores. IO-bound tasks (DB queries, HTTP calls) benefit from concurrency: while one thread waits for IO, others use the CPU. CPU-bound tasks (encryption, sorting) benefit from parallelism: multiple cores computing simultaneously.

Thread count: IO-bound → `cores × (1 + waitTime/computeTime)` (many threads). CPU-bound → `cores` (adding more causes context switching overhead). NEVER use one pool for both — IO tasks block threads, starving CPU tasks. Use separate pools: IO pool with many threads, CPU pool with cores threads. In banking: EOD batch with one 4-thread pool → DB queries occupied all threads → encryption queued for 10 minutes. Separate pools: 50-thread IO pool + 4-thread CPU pool → EOD time: 3 hours → 20 minutes.

---

keyPoints: Concurrency: managing multiple tasks, interleaving on single core
Parallelism: executing simultaneously on multiple cores
IO-bound: benefits from concurrency. CPU-bound: benefits from parallelism
